about: The AI pieces of the ecosystem: the Smart Graph, its MCP server, the Nuclear Developer, the Builder, how they work together and how the knowledge base is kept in step with the code.

rows.title: AI in NuclearLang: the Smart Graph, the Nuclear Developer and the Builder
rows.summary: Four pieces take a spec to tested, reviewed code on your machine: the Smart Graph (a private knowledge base), the MCP server `nuclear-mcp`, the Nuclear Developer (local agents on models of at most 3B parameters) and the Builder (the pipeline). A frontier model can lead; the local agents write.
body: | Piece | What it is | Where it runs |
| Nuclear Smart Graph | the knowledge base of the whole ecosystem, searched instead of guessing | `127.0.0.1:7878` |
| The MCP server (`nuclear-mcp`) | gives any agent the graph, the compiler, a project's commands, the generators and the local developer | started by the AI client, over stdio |
| Nuclear Developer | the local agents: coder, tester, security reviewer, planner, analyst, documenter, diagnoser, acceptor, assistant | `127.0.0.1:7879` |
| The Builder | the pipeline from a spec to deployed code: specification, generate, plan, tests first, code, verification, security, artifacts, deploy | the editor, or `nuclear-builder` |

| Nuclear Chat | the factory's workplace: channels, direct messages and threads with the members of your teams, who answer through their providers (a team's tech lead for the team) | `127.0.0.1:7880`, a token from the keyring |

The idea: a small model cannot hold much in its head, so what it needs comes from the graph, and what it writes is checked by the compiler before it answers. Standard code is written by generators, not by a model. A frontier model (Claude, or any other over MCP) is the lead: it plans, validates and corrects only what is wrong, and what it corrects becomes an example the local agents learn from.

Everything local runs on your machine: the models on Ollama, the graph and the Developer on `127.0.0.1`. It goes to the internet only when you choose a frontier model to lead, import a spec from Jira or GitHub, read an API's answer or documentation, or deploy.
Set up once: `nuclear-builder setup` (the installer's last step; VS Code has it as a wizard). It suggests the models that fit the machine, installs everything and starts the services at every login.

rows.title: The Nuclear Smart Graph: the knowledge base of the ecosystem
rows.summary: The Smart Graph is the local, private library of everything NuclearLang is: typed cards on shelves (concepts, language, platforms, tools, errors, capabilities, playbooks, examples, docs), linked to each other, searched by meaning and by exact name, with the exact facts of the ecosystem in a relational database for the questions that have one right answer. Agents ask it instead of guessing.
body: - **Shelves.** Each shelf answers one kind of question: *concepts* (what, why, how), *language* (how it is written), *platforms* (kinds, decorators, layout), *tools* (every command, MCP tool, route, generator, agent), *errors* (what went wrong and its fix), *capabilities* (what can and cannot be done), *playbooks* (how a task is done, step by step), *examples* (validated code) and *docs* (the long documents).

- **Cards.** A row is one card with a stable id (`error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `tool:nuclear.gen.resource`), a title, a summary, a body and links to other cards. A card can be fetched by its id, with no search.
- **A graph.** Cards link to each other with typed edges: an error to the errors it comes with and to its fix, a kind to its decorators, a playbook to the tools of its steps.

- **Hybrid search.** A query is matched by meaning (a local embeddings model) and by the exact names it writes (`N0114`, `gen resource`, `usecase`), and a card is also found by the questions it answers. The search is exact: every card a filter matches is compared with the question, so a card the graph holds is always found.

- **Exact answers.** A question that asks which, how many or what are (every tool of the MCP server, the parameters of a tool, the commands that create a kind, what a diagnostic means, the stages of the Builder) is not answered by meaning: the graph keeps the names and structured fields of every card in a relational database (SQLite, in memory only, made from the sealed cards) and a catalogue of exact questions (the `queries` shelf), each with the query that answers it. A planner matches the question to the catalogue and to the shelves: the query runs only when its exact question is closer to what was asked than the closest card, so "what is nuclear" gets its card and not the commands of the tool of that name. It fills the query's parameters from the question's own words and runs it, with no model: the answer is every row, the same every time. Nuclear Atlas shows those rows as they are, under the assistant's explanation.
- **Two readers.** A local agent reads only Nuclear (`agents`); a frontier model also reads the dialects underneath, the decisions and the state.
- **Private.** It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, refuses web pages, gives nothing without a token the user allowed, and stores its texts encrypted.
- **Versioned.** The base has a schema and a revision; a check fails when it is behind the code.

Use it: `nuclear-graph search "<question>"`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"` (the exact rows, then the cards), `nuclear-graph card <id>`, `nuclear-graph stats`; from an AI client, the MCP tools `graph_search`, `graph_answer` and `graph_card`. The graph itself is written in Nuclear (the `python` dialect).

rows.title: The MCP of NuclearLang: what it is and how it works
rows.summary: MCP is the Model Context Protocol: the open protocol through which an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) starts a program and calls its tools. `nuclear-mcp` is that program for NuclearLang: it gives the client the generators, the local developer, the Smart Graph, the compiler, the `nuclear` commands and the internet as tools.
body: **How it works.** The AI client starts `nuclear-mcp` and talks to it over stdio. The server offers tools and a set of instructions; the instructions send a model that knows nothing about Nuclear to `nuclear_start` first (what Nuclear is, the rules, the work cycle on this machine, the atlas of every topic, each read with `nuclear_doc`). The model calls a tool, the server runs it on your machine (a search in the graph, `nuclear check`, `nuclear gen`, a request to the local agents) and answers text the model reads.
**Connect it.**
```sh
nuclear-builder setup                                # once: the AI services, and MCP clients' access to the graph
claude mcp add --scope user nuclear -- nuclear-mcp   # Claude Code
codex mcp add nuclear -- nuclear-mcp                 # Codex

Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`) and OpenCode (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`): an MCP server whose command is `nuclear-mcp`. VS Code's *Settings and integrations* (`Ctrl+Alt+S`) adds it with a button.
**Its tools, by group.**
- Learning Nuclear: `nuclear_start` (the first call), `nuclear_doc` (one topic of the atlas).
- The generators: `project_inspect`, `generate_component`, `generate_resource`, `generate_usecase`, `generate_screen`, `api_inspect`.
- The local developer: `developer_task`, `developer_retry`, `developer_review`, `developer_code`, `developer_test`, `developer_security`.

- The graph: `graph_strategy` (which kind of request it is and the plan of that kind: the first call after `nuclear_start`), `graph_answer`, `graph_search`, `graph_card`, `graph_prompt`, `graph_remember`, `graph_monitor` (the hot spots of the last run with `--monitor`, kept for later).

- The compiler and the command line: `project_monitor` (where the app is slow: the report of `nuclear run --monitor`), `nuclear_check`, `nuclear_build`, `nuclear_fmt`, `nuclear_help`, `nuclear_brief`, `nuclear_defs`, `nuclear_project` (new, build, install, test, check, analyze, make, gen, migrate, add, remove, explain).
- The internet: `web_search`, `web_read`.

**The way of working it asks for.** The generators write the standard code; the local developer does the rest first (`developer_task`); the frontier model validates (`nuclear_check`, `nuclear test`), corrects only what is wrong and records its review (`developer_review`), so the local agents learn from the correction.
Each tool has its row: `mcp:generate_resource`, `mcp:developer_task`... and the whole server is `mcp:server`.

A machine set up for remote agents only (`limit:remote-agents-only`) has the Smart Graph but no local developer: the server then offers the `graph_*` tools but no `developer_*` tool, and tells the model to write what the generators do not.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer: the local AI agents
rows.summary: The Nuclear Developer is a team of local agents on models of at most 3B parameters (on Ollama): a coder, a tester, a security reviewer, a planner, an analyst, a documenter, a diagnoser, an acceptor and a chat assistant. Each follows fixed steps: recall from the Smart Graph, write, check with the compiler, repair.
body: It is the junior developer of a frontier model: it writes one small piece well when the task is precise, and it does not make architecture decisions. It is itself a Synapsis backend written in Nuclear.
**Why it works with a small model.**
- A small model follows fixed steps better than it chooses tools, so each agent is a graph of fixed steps.
- What the model cannot remember comes from the Smart Graph: the card of the kind it writes, validated examples, the mistakes to avoid.
- What it writes is checked by the compiler before it answers; an error goes back to it with its card, at most three times.
- Standard code is not written by the model at all: the generators write it.
- It reads the project by itself: the files that declare the names its order writes are its context.
- Its answer is held to the order's own words: a name, a call or a value the order writes and the answer lacks is asked for once more.
- It reads and writes only Nuclear, never the target language.

**The agents** (each has its row: `agent:coder`, `agent:tester`...): the coder writes one `.nuc` file; the tester writes the tests; the security reviewer reports findings; the planner splits a spec into pieces of one file; the analyst says which kind of request a spec is; the documenter writes what a run did; the diagnoser says why a step failed and what to do; the acceptor holds each acceptance criterion against what a run left; the assistant answers Nuclear Atlas, the editor's chat.
**Roles.** Developer is one of its faces. It also works as tester, security reviewer, planner, documenter and support (`role:developer`, `role:tester`, `role:security`, `role:devops`...).

**It knows its limits.** One file per call, an 8192-token window by default, no decisions. Its plan says what of a spec the platform cannot do yet or is beyond a local model; a task beyond it is split smaller, handed to a frontier model that leads, or asked back to the user (`limit:agent-reasoning`, `playbook:escalate`).

Run it: `nuclear-developer` (it listens on `127.0.0.1:7879`); its models: `qwen2.5-coder:3b` writes code, `gemma4:e2b` plans and reviews, and the chat answers with its own small one (`CHAT_MODEL`, `qwen3.5:2b`).

rows.title: The set-up of the AI services: a profile of models for the machine
rows.summary: One set-up installs the Smart Graph, the Nuclear Developer and the models: `nuclear-builder setup` in a terminal, a wizard in VS Code, the last step of the installer. It reads the machine, suggests a profile (`lite`, `medium`, `hard`, or `remote`: remote agents only), says how far each works, and starts the graph, the Developer and Nuclear Chat at every login. The user chooses what is downloaded.
body: **The profiles.** The suggested one is the heaviest that runs well with the machine's memory and disk; a tight one and one that does not fit are marked with the reason, and may still be chosen.
| Profile | Models | Downloads | Memory | Measured |
| `lite` | `qwen2.5-coder:1.5b` | 1.6 GB | 8 GB (4 GB at least) | not measured yet |

| `medium` | `qwen2.5-coder:3b`; the chat `qwen3.5:2b` | 5.2 GB | 12 GB (8 GB at least) | as coder, the model of hard: 43 of 45 single-file tasks, 16 of 18 never seen; as assistant, 6 of the first 8 chat questions (hard: 10 of 10) |

| `hard` | `qwen2.5-coder:3b` + `gemma4:e2b`; the chat `qwen3.5:2b` | 12.4 GB | 24 GB (16 GB at least) | 43 of 45 single-file tasks (Claude Sonnet: 39), 16 of 18 never seen, 2 of 3 whole features, 10 of 10 chat questions, 10 of 11 analyses |
| `remote` | none | the Smart Graph's model (0.3 GB) | 2 GB | only the Smart Graph runs on the machine, with the MCP server |

Every profile also downloads the Smart Graph's own model (EmbeddingGemma in ONNX, 0.3 GB, in the figures above), which the graph runs itself: not Ollama's. The chat answers with one small model of its own (`CHAT_MODEL`; `lite` uses its one model), loaded only while you chat and freed 3 minutes after.

**What the set-up needs**, found by itself once installed or installed in a terminal the user sees: NuclearLang with its AI archive (a Python of its own with the services and the set-up, written in Nuclear: no Python, uv or Node.js on the machine) and Ollama (it runs the models; only the local profiles need it). From the source tree it also needs `uv`.

**Where things are.** The choice: `~/.config/nuclearlang/ai.env` (`%APPDATA%\nuclearlang\ai.env`): the mode, the profile, its models; the services start with it, and the Builder and the editor take their default models from it. The code of the services: `~/.local/share/nuclearlang/ai/`. The graph's data: `~/.local/share/nuclear-graph/`. The models: Ollama's own folder; the graph's, `~/.local/share/nuclear-graph/models/`.

**The services at login.** Linux: the systemd user units `nuclear-graph`, `nuclear-developer` and `nuclear-chat` (`systemctl --user status|restart ...`, `journalctl --user -u nuclear-graph`). macOS: three launch agents (`io.github.nuclearlang.graph`, `.developer`, `.chat`). Windows: a script of the Startup folder. In idle both take about 150 MB of memory; Ollama loads a model when an agent asks and frees it a few minutes later.

**Update and remove.** Running the installer again sets the services up again with the same profile, without questions. `nuclear-builder setup --remove` takes the services away; Ollama, its models and the graph's data stay (`--remove --all`, and the installer's `--uninstall`: everything it made).

**The ports.** `127.0.0.1:7878` the graph, `7879` the Developer, `7880` Nuclear Chat; a port another program holds is replaced by the next free one, written to `ai.env` (`NUCLEAR_GRAPH_PORT`, `NUCLEAR_DEVELOPER_PORT`, `NUCLEAR_CHAT_PORT`). Nuclear Chat's token is made the first time and kept only in the keyring; a host reads it with `nuclear-chat connect --json`.

rows.title: The Nuclear Builder: the software factory from a spec to a pull request
rows.summary: The Builder takes a spec through six stations on your machine (Analysis, Design, Tests first, Code, Quality, Delivery), each worked by a role of the run's team: the local agents, a provider's agent or a provider's model. It stops at its gates for you, documents every station in the spec's folder (`specs/<component>[/<layer>]/<id>/`), and any station or step can run again.
body: 1. **Analysis** (Analyst): the spec read as the client's request, the acceptance criteria made checkable, the questions to answer first; the analysis decides the strategy and the stations that run (`concept:strategies`). `analysis.md`, `questions.md`.

2. **Design** (Architect): the generators write first what follows from the data (`nuclear gen resource`); then the design, its Mermaid diagrams and ADRs, and a plan of one-file pieces. `design.md`, `plan.md`.
3. **Tests first** (Developer): the tests from the acceptance criteria and the plan, before any code. `test-plan.md`.

4. **Code** (Developer): what the generators did not write; each use case wired by `nuclear gen usecase`; repaired with the compiler (`nuclear fix`, then `nuclear check` errors to the agent); the lead takes what is left.

5. **Quality** (QA): its plan goes into the run's checks and stops for you (switch checks, add your own, run yours); then the build and the tests, up to three repair rounds told by `nuclear explain`, the acceptance criteria held against the result. `qa-report.md`.

6. **Delivery** (DevOps): the definition of done, the user stories and the pull request's text, and the infrastructure the change needs (the CI exported from the line, the deployments and environments, the containers, the monitoring, the secrets); once you approve, the branch, the commit in your name and the pull request with `gh`, never merged.

- **The team** is the members the user hires, any number per role, each worked by the local agents, a provider's agent or an API model (`nuclear-builder team …`, the new-team wizard in VS Code; no presets, ADR-platform-0010); a station is worked by the member the tech lead assigned, else the role's first. One budget per run (5 USD by default); anything paid is confirmed twice unless the user turned that off, and `forceConfirm` brings the questions back.
- **Where**: VS Code (`Ctrl+Alt+P`), Android Studio (`Alt+Shift+P`), a terminal (`nuclear-builder run specs/<component>/<id>/spec.md`), or over MCP (`developer_task`).
- **The gates**: after Analysis, Design and before Delivery by default (`.nuclear/builder.json` `gates`); `nuclear-builder run --resume <id>` goes on.
- **The journal**: `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.md`, next to the run file `<id>.json` the editors draw.

- **When it fails**: the diagnoser says why; `nuclear-builder retry <id>` goes on from the station that failed, `--from <station>` from another, `--step <step>` from one step with every step after it; `nuclear-builder restart <id>` runs it all again. What the steps left out wrote is undone first; a file changed since is kept.
- **On a server**: `nuclear-builder ci` runs the commands of `.nuclear/builder.json` and `nuclear-builder export github|gitlab|bitbucket` writes the CI file.

rows.title: Local first: the generators and the local developer work, a frontier model leads
rows.summary: The order of work is fixed: the generators write the standard code, the local developer writes what is left, and a frontier model (Claude Sonnet, Opus, Haiku or any other) acts as the manager: it plans, validates and corrects only what failed. Its corrections become examples for the local agents.
body: A lead hands work to a junior the same way:
1. **The lead understands the whole** (the spec, the project, the architecture) and splits the work into small orders: one file, one declaration, every name given.
2. **The tools write what is standard**: `generate_resource` for every resource the spec names; `generate_usecase` wires each use case the local developer wrote (its alias in the facade, its route).
3. **The local developer writes each small piece** without needing the whole picture: its order names the path, the kind, the names it must use and the files it depends on.
4. **The lead validates**: `nuclear_check` of the project and `nuclear test`.
5. **The lead corrects only what is wrong**, never what passed, and records it (`developer_review`): the corrected files become examples in the graph.

Without a frontier model the local agents do every step themselves (`--lead local`). That works for specs written with the platform's words and for standard features; for a spec in plain words or a feature of several files with its own design, a lead is needed.

Why this order: the cheapest worker that can do a step does it. A generator costs nothing and never fails; a local model costs seconds of your CPU; a frontier model costs money, so it is used for what only it can do: understanding and judgment.

rows.title: How the knowledge base stays in step with the code: assets, revisions and the check
rows.summary: The knowledge base is asset files in `nuclear-developer/data`: most rows are generated from the working tree, the rest are written by hand and name their sources. It has a schema and a revision; `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a row is behind the code, and every finished feature ends with build, check and ingest.
body: - **Generated rows** are read from a structured source and never edited: the compiler's diagnostics, the standard library, each platform's kinds, decorators and layout, the help of the four CLIs, the MCP tools, the HTTP routes, the Builder's stages, the agents, the editor's commands, each component's version, the example projects and every document section. They cannot drift: building again rewrites them.

- **Curated rows** are written by hand (the purpose, the concepts, the playbooks, the capabilities, the failures). Each names the `sources` it was written from. When a source changes, the check asks for a review of that row.
- **Overlays** add hand-written fields (links, examples, questions) to generated rows.

- **Versions.** `manifest.json` holds the schema (the row format), the revision (it rises by one whenever any row changes) and, per row, its hash and the revision that last changed it. `revisions.json` is the log. The graph remembers the revision it ingested.
The commands:
```sh
nuclear-graph knowledge build     # write the generated assets, validate everything, raise the revision
nuclear-graph knowledge check     # fail when the assets, a curated row or the graph are behind the tree
nuclear-graph knowledge review    # record that a curated row still holds after its source changed
nuclear-graph ingest              # the graph learns the new revision (only what changed is embedded)
A build refuses an invalid base: a link to a row that does not exist, a duplicated id, or target-language code in a row the local agents read.
The rule for whoever changes the ecosystem (a person or an agent): a feature is not done until `knowledge check` is clean and the graph holds the new revision.

rows.title: Strategies: how the agent decides what to do with a request
rows.summary: Each kind of request a user makes has a strategy: a row that says how the kind is recognised, its plan with the tool of every step and what it asks of a run. No model chooses it: the request's exact signs decide, then its meaning. 31 kinds, from a whole system to a failing test.
body: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way. So before anything is generated or planned, the **analyst** says which kind of request it is, and the run follows the strategy of that kind (ADR-developer-0001).
| Family | Strategies |

| create | `strategy:system`, `strategy:project`, `strategy:component`, `strategy:resource-api`, `strategy:resource-db`, `strategy:client-of-backend`, `strategy:interface`, `strategy:repository`, `strategy:usecase`, `strategy:endpoint`, `strategy:declaration` |
| change | `strategy:member`, `strategy:refactor-rename`, `strategy:refactor-move-extract`, `strategy:refactor-architecture`, `strategy:data-migration`, `strategy:configuration`, `strategy:remove` |
| fix | `strategy:bug-compile`, `strategy:bug-failing-test`, `strategy:bug-behaviour`, `strategy:bug-runtime`, `strategy:bug-data-contract`, `strategy:bug-interface`, `strategy:bug-environment` |
| verify and explain | `strategy:tests`, `strategy:security-review`, `strategy:document`, `strategy:question`, `strategy:operate` |
| beyond | `strategy:beyond` |

**How a kind is recognised.** By the request's exact signs first (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>` line, a `VERB /path` line), then by its words and its meaning, and by whether the project already has the names it writes. The answer says which signs chose it.

**What a strategy decides.** The stages of the Builder that run (a compile error needs no Generate, a rename no tests first); where the pieces come from (the planner, the files that declare what changes, or a tool that already rewrote them); the generators it calls; the facts it cannot start without, asked to the user instead of guessed; whether it needs a frontier model to lead.

**Tools before models.** In every strategy a generator writes what is standard, the compiler's exact fixes come before any repair, a rename is done by a tool, and a model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.
**Ask it.** `nuclear-graph strategy "<request>"` in a terminal; `graph_strategy` over MCP; the Analysis step of a Builder run. A spec may name its strategy itself: `- Strategy: usecase`.

rows.title: The software factory: stations, roles as files, providers as assignments, teams
rows.summary: Every spec goes through six stations, each owned by a role: Analysis (Analyst), Design (Architect), Tests first and Code (Developer), Quality (QA), Delivery (DevOps: the infrastructure and the delivery; its id `delivery` of before is read as `devops`). A role is a folder of files, nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/, that the local agents and every provider read; who does a role is the user's choice.
body: Spec 011 and ADR-platform-0005 make Nuclear Builder a **software factory**: the same stations, in the same order, for every spec.
| Station | Role | What it delivers (in `specs/<id>/`) |
| Analysis | Analyst | `analysis.md` (the acceptance criteria made checkable), `questions.md` |
| Design | Architect | `design.md` (components, diagrams, the ADRs it follows), proposed ADRs, `plan.md` |
| Tests first, Code | Developer | the tests (TDD), then the code; `work-log.md` |
| Quality | QA | `test-plan.md` first, for the user to approve; then `qa-report.md` (functional and non-functional checks, edge cases, security, good practices, load and performance) |

| Delivery | DevOps | `definition-of-done.md`, `user-stories.md`, the project's documents, `pr.md`, `deployment.md` when the change touches the CI, the deployments, the containers, the monitoring or the secrets; pushes only when the user approves and never merges |

**A role is a folder** (`nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/`, ADR-developer-0002): `role.md` (mission, inputs, outputs, definition of done, what it never does), `skills/*.md`, `templates/*.md`, `checks.toml` (each check on or off, at a station, run by the role or by the user), and `roster/{en,es}.json` (the 40 satirical employees the user hires for it, each with a temperament of `roles/temperaments.json`: extrovert, shy, nerd…) with their painted cyberpunk portraits in `roster/faces/<id>.webp`, made by a local image model (FLUX.1-schnell through stable-diffusion.cpp) that `roles/faces.nuc` drives from each employee's profile, temperament and gender (ADR-developer-0003).

**The prompts of the local agents are the roles' skills**: a skill whose front matter names a prompt (`prompt: agent.repair`) is ingested into the graph's `prompts` collection, so `graph_prompt` and the Nuclear Developer read the same text. A change to one is a new evaluation round.

**Who does a role** is an assignment: the local agents (models of at most 3B), a provider's agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode) or a provider's model through an API, chosen per member of a **team**. A team (ADR-platform-0010) is the members the user hires from the rosters, any number per role (twenty developers if so), one of them the tech lead; it is made with a five-step wizard (identity with a suggested name, purpose and skills, members suggested from them, the roster with filters, who works each member with every paid one marked), never from a preset. A station is worked by the member the tech lead assigned for the run (`run --assign`), else the role's first member; one budget per run, confirmed twice before any money is spent.

**Skills are real files** (spec 011 requirement 34): the library `nuclear-agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` (Claude Code's format; domains such as payments, bank accounts, authentication, offline sync; technologies such as the Synapsis backend, mobile and web, WebSockets, SQL, Ollama, CI; practices such as TDD, an OWASP review, clean architecture) and `nuclear-agents/agents/<id>/agent.md` (backend, mobile and web engineers, a QA security tester, a tech writer). A team attaches library skills (`skills`) every member inherits and keeps its own (`ownSkills`, cloned or written in the skills editor); a member has the same and a base `agent`.
